bio.en: Ben Williams is VP of Product at Snyk, where he built the company's developer-growth organization and helped scale the developer-first security platform from an early-stage startup into an $8.6B-valued leader serving millions of developers.
bio.zh: Ben Williams 是 Snyk 的产品副总裁，他在那里搭建了公司的开发者增长组织，并帮助这家“开发者优先”的安全平台从早期初创公司成长为估值 86 亿美元、服务数百万开发者的行业领军者。

summary.en: Snyk's early growth came from a narrow, developer-first wedge—starting with Node.js open-source security and winning the Node community through conferences, content, and a free CLI—before expanding languages and adding enterprise governance features. A defining lesson is that self-serve monetization stalled until the team built 'table stakes' enterprise features and leaned into product-led sales, while powerful growth loops (GitHub fix PRs, Snyk Advisor, security education) kept fueling acquisition and activation. Ben details how to run an effective growth org: cross-functional, outcome-based teams (acquisition/activation/monetization/platform), a 'decision science' function, and a loop-based growth model documented qualitatively and quantified quarterly. He also shares a crisp framework for vision/mission, practical advice on freemium packaging and activation metrics (a team fixing a vulnerability within 30 days), plus his favorite tools and books.
summary.zh: Snyk 早期的增长来自一个又窄又“开发者优先”的楔子——从 Node.js 开源安全起步，通过会议、内容和免费的命令行工具赢得 Node 社区——之后才扩展语言并加上企业级治理功能。一个关键教训是：在团队构建出“桌面筹码”级的企业功能、并转向产品驱动销售之前，自助变现一直停滞；而强大的增长闭环（GitHub 修复 PR、Snyk Advisor、安全教育）持续为获取和激活供能。Ben 详细讲了怎么运营一个有效的增长组织：跨职能、按结果组织的团队（获取/激活/变现/平台）、一个“决策科学”职能，以及一个定性记录、按季度量化的闭环式增长模型。他还分享了一个清晰的愿景/使命框架、关于免费增值打包和激活指标（一个团队在 30 天内修复一个漏洞）的实用建议，以及他最喜欢的工具和数据/书籍。

So, eventually, getting back to your original question, that's all of the context and where and when and how they did it, but the first hundred or so users really just came from the founders engaging with the Node.js community and the interest that drove. turns.zh: 对，就是回看整个市场。当时，PLG（产品驱动增长）或者自下而上，和“安全”这两个词，从来没人把它们放在同一个句子里说过，对吧？安全一直是个中心化的职能。历史上的安全项目更多是审计、监管和 enforcement，而不是赋能开发者。你看到的销售动作也一直是自上而下的。它被视为不可动摇的——CISO 和其他应用安全负责人才是买家。当时市面上的安全工具，全都是为这种格局服务的，而且这些工具拖慢了开发者的速度，制造了大量挫败感，也遭遇了很多抵触，对于持续的采用和强烈的参与度、留存来说，这绝不是理想的配方。基于那些方案的安全项目，最终也没能达到真正需要的有效性。(00:10:46) 正是基于这种认识，再叠加当时 DevOps 带来的相邻市场变化，催生了 Snyk 背后的想法。创始人 Guy、Danny 和 Assaf 看到了一个真正去用不同方式做事的机会。他们相信，提升应用安全态势最有效的途径，是一条开发者优先的路。他们知道，开发者越来越在意自己代码的安全性，就像在意性能和功能质量一样。但他们也知道，要赋能开发者去掌握这种安全性，他们需要比以往好得多、摩擦小得多的工具。而他们的做法，回过头看我觉得超级聪明——聚焦社区。那还不算我们现在理解的完整的社区驱动增长，但已经很接近了。(00:11:35) 他们一开始的聚焦非常窄。单一人物画像、单一场景、单一用例。对 Snyk 来说，这意味着：用 Node.js 构建应用、并且希望确保自己引入的开源依赖是安全的开发者。开源软件，是构建现代软件时一个巨大的加速器。今天一个普通的应用，至少有 75% 是开源库和组件。所以，这越来越成为一个主要的攻击向量——恶意攻击者可以在一个开源组件里找到一个漏洞，然后在每一个用到这个组件的应用里找到它并加以利用。与此同时，至少在当年，开源软件在安全漏洞方面的测试要少得多，而开源库的维护者往往安全意識也比较弱。有了这个背景，再看当时 Node.js 作为运行环境正在获得牵引力，企业里的采用越来越多，专门的会议也越来越多，但社区还足够小，Snyk 还能真正去影响它。于是 Guy 和其他人就在那个社区里全力以赴了。他们在开发者大会、meetup 上做分享，制作线上内容，等等。他们反复向社区抛出的问题是：你的应用里有已知漏洞吗？而 Snyk 就在那里帮他们回答这个问题。顺便说个有趣的小知识：如果你在 Urban Dictionary 里搜 Snyk，你会看到它是“so now you know”的缩写。但所有这些能够奏效，我认为归根结底是因为并行的产品驱动打法。所以，虽然“你的产品怎么从用户身上赚钱”这个问题在 Snyk 早期远没有清晰答案，但“你的产品怎么获取和留住用户”这个问题的答案，一直是产品驱动的。(00:13:35) Snyk 最早那个版本，是一个命令行工具。它是给开发者用的工具，可以本地运行，也可以轻松集成到 CI/CD 流水线里做早期反馈。它让开发者能为自己应用的安全承担更多责任，这和那些由安全团队在开发后期才运行、反馈周期长、问题被“扔过墙”的传统技术完全不同，后者只会不可避免地让开发者抓狂。而这一切都建立在一个根本信念上：对于以软件为中心的组织来说，要想持续有效地应对“变得并始终保持安全”这个挑战，唯一可行的路径——我说的可行，是真的指可持续地有效——就是走这条开发者主导的路。所以，这本质上是对行业的彻底颠覆，也正因如此，赢得开发者的采用一直是我们的关键优先级。(00:14:31) 基于这个思路，Snyk 从第一天起就以某种形式免费可用，早期策略始终是：创造有价值、随手可得、用独特差异化方式解决真实问题的东西，并让它无处不在。有了开发者主导这个核心，免费增值的 go-to-market 策略就成了理所当然的选择。所以，说回你最初的问题——这就是所有的背景，以及他们在哪里、什么时候、怎么做成了这件事。但最初的一百来个用户，真的就来自创始人和 Node.js 社区的互动，以及由此带来的兴趣。我想在开始任何变现尝试之前，我们大概已经有大约 5000 个免费用户了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. There's a bunch I want to unpack there because what's interesting the way you describe it maps to the series that I recently wrote about consumer growth strategy and how the first three steps after you have an idea is to come up with your super specific who, kind of your target persona, come up with a hook that catches them and gets them excited, and then go find them where they are and pitch them your hook. So, the super specific who for Snyk was you said open source developers working on Node.js. Is that right?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这里有很多我想展开聊的，因为你描述的方式，恰好对应我最近写的那篇关于消费级增长策略的文章——有了一个想法之后，前三个步骤是：想清楚你极其具体的“谁”，也就是目标人物画像；想一个能勾住他们、让他们兴奋的“钩子”；然后去他们所在的地方，把你的钩子抛给他们。所以 Snyk 那个极其具体的“谁”，就像你说的，是做 Node.js 的开源开发者。对吗？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Well, it was Node.js developers, and Node.js developers were building their applications using open source Node components.
turns.zh: 嗯，是 Node.js 开发者，而且是用开源 Node 组件来构建应用的开发者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm. Got it. Was there any other constraint to that, do you know, or those were the two to three attributes of a user?
turns.zh: 嗯哼，明白了。你还知道有没有别的限制条件？还是说这就是一个用户的两三个属性？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: That's really it. The community was growing for sure. It was big enough to have a decent opportunity there-
turns.zh: 主要就是这些。那个社区肯定是在增长的，大到已经算是个不错的机会了——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Makes sense.
turns.zh: 有道理。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: ... but narrow enough that technology wise, it meant that a product could be brought to market in a reasonable time.
turns.zh: ——但又足够窄，从技术角度看，意味着一个产品能在合理时间内推向市场。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's great. And then the hook was basically you have known vulnerabilities in your code base which if I were an engineer, like, "I don't know, shoot, I don't know. Get a find exactly. I'm scared now."
turns.zh: 对，这很好。然后那个钩子基本上就是“你的代码库里有已知漏洞”，要是我一个工程师，我大概会想：“我不知道啊，糟了，我也不知道。赶紧帮我查查。我现在害怕了。”

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Exactly. And then so now you know. Right?
turns.zh: 没错。然后，“so now you know”，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. Okay, cool. And then the where, so you said that they went to open source communities. Do you have any more specifics about what those were? Was it like a specific forum? Was it like GitHub somewhere? Was it Reddit? Do you know any idea where those communities lived?
turns.zh: 对，没错。好，酷。然后“在哪里”——你说他们去了开源社区。你还能说得更具体一点吗？是某个特定的论坛？是 GitHub 的某个地方？还是 Reddit？你知道那些社区具体在哪里吗？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Yeah, it was less about a particular place, but more about the community of developers themselves who focused on Node.js. So, a bunch of early evangelism was really at conferences. It was I think the Velocity Conference in Amsterdam where Guy and Assaf kind of first unveiled Snyk to the world, and yeah, it went from there.
turns.zh: 嗯，它更少是关于某个具体的地方，更多是关乎那些专注 Node.js 的开发者社区本身。所以早期的布道，很多是在会议上。我记得是在阿姆斯特丹的 Velocity Conference，Guy 和 Assaf 第一次把 Snyk 介绍给全世界，然后从那里扩散开来的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see. Interesting. So, it was in-person events, conferences, and meetups probably focused on Node.js developers.
turns.zh: 我明白了。有意思。所以是在线下活动、会议，以及大概聚焦 Node.js 开发者的 meetup 上。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Exactly. Yeah.
turns.zh: 对，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, awesome. What happened after that? So, that was the first hundred. Was it just roughly the next stage of growth or did it focus on that for a long time? What was the next stage roughly?
turns.zh: 好，太棒了。那之后发生了什么？那就是最初的一百个。是大致进入下一个增长阶段，还是在这个点上停留了很久？下一个阶段大概是什么样的？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Yeah. I think that focus was the really important kind of element there, if I can kind of latch on that. Starting with that narrow focus and building around community engagement, I think it's a well-proven playbook now, particularly in the developer tooling space like New Relic did it notably with Ruby community for example. But ultimately it was important because of this kind of depth verse breadth approach and that depth-first approach that Snyk took was important to be able to effectively validate the solution on the path to product market fit. A JavaScript developer just won't care if you support Golang or Rust, but will absolutely care if a key feature like automated package upgrades just isn't available for their ecosystem. (00:18:04): Of course, the bigger problem of vulnerable components in open source across all languages and all ecosystems, that's a very widespread problem. It affects the industry at large, but that just spoke to the potential opportunity that was there to be unlocked. But the key for Snyk I think was just not to go too wide, too early. So, it focused on nailing that initial use case for that specific community of Node.js devs, like I say, narrow enough to be able to really focus on quickly building a compelling solution to a real problem, but also wide enough to be something viable from a growth perspective. And even back then the NPM, the Node Package Manager hosted around 200,000 open source packages. They were downloaded something like two and a half billion times a month by over 2 million devs. And the typical node app would have hundreds of dependencies, mostly indirect and so hidden less immediately visible. But each of those dependencies brought with it some security risks. So, yeah, I think nailing that narrow and deep-use case before expanding wider was absolutely critical and generally just sound advice around finding product market fit and building solid momentum before casting a wider net. It's difficult to maintain that focus for sure as the lure of that bigger term can be really tempting, but ultimately you have to build a service and market well to capture it.
turns.zh: 对。如果我可以抓住这点说一句的话，我觉得那个聚焦才是真正重要的元素。从那个窄聚焦起步，并围绕社区互动去构建，我认为现在已经是被验证过的打法了，尤其是在开发者工具领域，比如 New Relic 当年在 Ruby 社区就这么做得很出名。但最终它重要，是因为这种“深度优先 vs 广度优先”的思路。Snyk 采取的深度优先 approach，对于在通向产品市场契合（PMF）的路上有效验证解决方案很重要。一个 JavaScript 开发者根本不会在乎你支不支持 Golang 或 Rust，但他绝对会在意“自动化的包升级”这种关键功能在他的生态里就是没有。(00:18:04) 当然，跨所有语言和所有生态的开源漏洞这个更大的问题，是非常普遍的，影响整个行业。但这恰恰说明了那里有待释放的巨大机会。不过对 Snyk 来说，关键就是不要太早铺太开。所以，它专注于为那群特定的 Node.js 开发者搞定那个初始用例——就像我说的，窄到能真正聚焦、快速为真实问题构建出有说服力的方案，但又宽到从增长角度说是一件值得做的事。即便在当年，NPM（Node 包管理器）上托管着大约 20 万个开源包，每个月被超过 200 万开发者下载大约 25 亿次。一个典型的 Node 应用会有数百个依赖，大多还是间接的、因而隐藏起来不那么显眼。但每一个依赖都带来一些安全风险。所以，我认为在铺得更开之前，先搞定那个又窄又深的用例，绝对是关键，而且这本身就是一条关于寻找产品市场契合、在撒更大网之前先建立扎实势头的普适建议。要保持那种聚焦当然很难，因为那个更大蛋糕的诱惑真的很诱人，但你终究得先把服务和市唱好，才能接住它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a sense of when that focus expanded to an adjacent group, how many years into the growth story that happened, or was there some kind of milestone there? Because I know everyone imagines, yeah, we'll expand, the question is when and when does it make sense and when is it too early. Do you have any insights into that phase?
turns.zh: 你知道那个聚焦是什么时候扩展到相邻群体的吗？是在增长故事里过了多少年发生的，还是说有什么里程碑？因为大家都知道“对，我们会扩张”，问题是什么时候扩、什么时候合理、什么时候又太早。你对那个阶段有什么洞察？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Yeah, for sure. First, I think if we're talking about PLG and the story with Snyk, I actually like that definition of product-led acquisition from Julian Shapiro when you spoke with him, and beyond that maniacal focus on finding product market fit for your product, founders really should be thinking about how their product is going to grow, and that's important of course as you think about taking that next step. So, let's assume in a simplistic definition that you found product market fit as demonstrated by a strong retention, and then the real question is where are the new users for your product going to come from, and founders really should have, I think, strong hypothesis around this, your risk essentially, adopting an if we build it, they'll come approach. (00:20:27): So, if your acquisition strategy is product- led, then understanding and being intentional about your early acquisition growth loops I think is an essential founder's responsibility. Dedicating time there to design those loops into the product, it's key. And when I say product, I really mean the whole product experience considering every touchpoint in and out of the core application that your users and customers might have with you. Snyk, for example, believed very early that we could build out powerful content loops via fixed pull requests that we raise on GitHub. New users, they'll sign up for Snyk, they'll connect their GitHub accounts, Snyk will scan their code, will find vulnerabilities, will automatically create Snyk-branded pull requests to fix those vulnerabilities. Other devs in the repo will see and interact with those PRs, and some of them will follow links to Snyk, create accounts and some of them will connect their own repos, and so the loop continues. So, company generated, company distributed content loop, it's actually really powerful for us because it's both an acquisition loop and an engagement loop. (00:21:28): Over the course of time, we extended that loop by adding support for other source controlled systems beyond GitHub. We layered on a bunch of new loops, and I think if founders can be intentional about this as you're developing early product iterations, then you're going to have a bigger advantage when the product clicks with the market, and that was built into Snyk as we went along. So, that was kind of ready as we found product market fit. But I think to talk about specifically how Snyk took that next stage, it was a function of when we were chatting before this, we talked a little bit about some of the failed experiences spinning up a self-serve revenue channel, and-
turns.zh: 有，当然。首先，如果我们在聊 PLG 和 Snyk 的故事，我其实挺喜欢你跟 Julian Shapiro 聊时他给的“产品驱动获取”那个定义。除了那种对找到产品市场契合的疯魔般聚焦之外，创始人真的应该去思考他们的产品要怎么增长，而当你考虑迈出下一步时，这当然很重要。所以，我们先简单假设你已经找到了产品市场契合，表现为很强的留存，那么真正的问题就是：你产品的新用户会从哪里来？我认为创始人对此真的应该有很强的假设，而不是采取“我们造出来了，他们自然会来”这种碰运气的方式。(00:20:27) 所以，如果你的获取策略是产品驱动的，那么去理解并刻意设计你早期的“获取型增长闭环”，我认为是一个必不可少的开创者责任。在那里投入时间去把这些闭环设计进产品里，是关键。而我说“产品”的时候，指的是整个产品体验——考虑到用户和客户可能与你产生接触的所有触点，无论是在核心应用内还是外。以 Snyk 为例，我们很早就有一种信念：我们可以通过在 GitHub 上发起的 fix pull request 来构建强大的内容闭环。新用户注册 Snyk，连上他们的 GitHub 账号，Snyk 会扫描他们的代码、找出漏洞，并自动创建带 Snyk 品牌的 pull request 去修复那些漏洞。仓库里的其他开发者会看到这些 PR 并与之互动，其中一些人会顺着链接来到 Snyk、创建账号，有些人还会连上自己的仓库，于是闭环继续。(00:21:28) 随着时间推移，我们扩展了那个闭环，加入了对 GitHub 之外其他源代码管理系统的支持。我们又叠加了一堆新的闭环。我认为如果创始人能在早期产品迭代时就对这种事有意为之，那么当产品和市场对上频的时候，你就会有一个更大的优势——而这在 Snyk 是一路走来就内建进去的。所以等我们找到 PMF 时，它已经准备好了。但要具体聊 Snyk 是怎么迈出那下一步的，这要看我们之前聊过的一点——我们聊过一些启动自助收入渠道的失败经历，还有——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Actually before we get there, which I definitely want to get into all that, I love this story you just shared. I hadn't heard of this growth tactic of basically they connect their GitHub account, you find all the vulnerabilities, push a fix, people see that Snyk did this for them and it just provides all this value, and you're saying that was really effective. It's an example of something that worked very well.
turns.zh: 其实在你说到那之前——我特别想聊那些——你刚分享的这个策略我太喜欢了，之前没听过这种增长战术：他们连上 GitHub 账号，你找出所有漏洞，推一个修复，人们看到 Snyk 为他们做了这件事，就带来了巨大的价值，你说这非常有效。这是个做得很好的例子。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: First of all, that integration in terms of connecting your code with security scanning like that was a first of a kind integration.
turns.zh: 首先，那种把你的代码和安全扫描连接起来的集成，是史无前例的第一例集成。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, magic.
turns.zh: 对，像魔法一样。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: No one had done that before. But the key was that we ultimately controlled the content. So, not only was the fixed pull request doing something useful in terms of the code, but all of the description of the pull request was explaining about the vulnerability, educating users, and it was all Snyk branded and saying, "If you find this useful, click here, come and learn more about the vulnerability. Sign up for an account if you don't have one." It kept existing users coming back. PART 1 OF 4 ENDS [00:23:04]
turns.zh: 之前从没人这么做过。但关键在于，我们最终掌控了那个内容。所以，那个 fix pull request 不光在代码层面做了有用的事，而且整个 PR 的描述都在讲解那个漏洞、教育用户，并且全是 Snyk 品牌，写着“如果你觉得有用，点这里，来了解这个漏洞。如果你还没有账号就注册一个”。它让老用户持续回来。[00:23:04] 第 1 段 / 共 4 段 结束

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: You sign up for an account if you don't have one, it kept existing users coming back and it brings new users, a lot of new users, in fact.
turns.zh: 如果你还没有账号就注册一个，它让老用户持续回来，也带来新用户——事实上，是大量的新用户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You'd be in there all like, "Do you have known vulnerabilities in your code base? Click here to find out." Is that responsible for much of the early growth, that loop?

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: I think that was one of the loops. We also have a couple of, from fairly early on as well, other content loops that are more kind of programmatic SEO assets that have both been pretty instrumental in terms of new user growth, yeah.
turns.zh: 我觉得那是其中一个闭环。我们从相当早开始，也还有另外几个内容闭环，更多是那种程序化 SEO 资产，在新用户增长方面也都相当管用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It'd be cool to hear about those if they're relatively straightforward to explain, and then we can get to the thing that didn't work, the self-serve monetization piece you were going to get to.
turns.zh: 如果能相对好懂地讲讲那些就太酷了，然后我们再聊那个没奏效的东西——你准备讲的自助变现那块。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: We have a bunch of loops actually at this point to start off.
turns.zh: 到这个阶段我们其实有一堆闭环了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Lucky you.
turns.zh: 你真走运。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Yeah, I'm a big loopist, funnily enough. But yeah, we have a bunch of loops. Company generated, company distributed content loops have actually worked really well for us. We have a side car product called Snyk Advisor. Snyk Advisor, it's basically a service that developers use to search and find open source packages when they're considering integrating some within their software applications. The unique thing about it is it indexes all of the package managers. It learns about those packages. It augments the data about them with a bunch of metadata, including of course Snyk security scans, but we also find out how actively maintained the software is on the source repo on GitHub or wherever. (00:24:31): We build this kind of package health score, so anyone searching on Google for a package that does X, Y, Z or a specific package by name, Snyk Advisor will be right up there in terms of the search results. They'll land on there, they'll get a good idea about that package, they can look at similar packages and it's all, of course, a Snyk website and we have CTAs to say, "If you want to secure your application on a perpetual basis, then just come and join us." That's a great loop. That's all kind of a programmatic asset. There are hundreds of thousands of these package pages, but they're just automatically being generated continuously.
turns.zh: 对，说来有趣，我是个重度“闭环主义者”。不过没错，我们有一堆闭环。公司生成、公司分发的内容闭环，对我们来说真的很好用。我们有个叫 Snyk Advisor 的副产品。Snyk Advisor 基本上是个服务，开发者在考虑把某些开源包集成进自己的软件应用时，可以用它来搜索和查找开源包。它独特的地方在于，它会索引所有的包管理器，学习那些包的信息，并用一堆元数据来增强关于它们的数据——当然包括 Snyk 的安全扫描，但我们也会查出来那个软件在 GitHub 或其他地方的源仓库上维护得有多活跃。(00:24:31) 我们做出一种“包健康分”，所以任何在 Google 上搜索“能做 X、Y、Z 的包”或者按名字搜某个具体包的人，Snyk Advisor 都会排在搜索结果很靠前的位置。他们落到这个页面上，对那个包有个清楚的认识，可以看相似的包，而这当然全都是 Snyk 的网站，我们也有 CTA 说“如果你想长期保障你的应用安全，那就来加入我们”。这是个很棒的闭环。这全都是程序化的资产。有几十万个这样的包页面，但它们是自动持续生成的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. It's programmatically generated better indexing of open source libraries that you can integrate with. That is so smart. It's programmatic because you can inform on the security vulnerabilities and then the maintenance and activity. Interesting. Yeah, that makes sense. That's all data you could just gather. That's awesome. Okay, so there's that. Is there anything else that's worked really well for you guys to help you grow self-serve?
turns.zh: 明白了。它是程序化生成的、对你能集成的开源库更好的索引。太聪明了。说它程序化，是因为你可以就漏洞以及维护活跃度提供信息。有意思。对，这说得通。那都是你能直接收集的数据。太棒了。好，所以有这个。还有别的什么对你们自助增长特别管用的吗？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: One of the recent ones that's really interesting is security education. We think of Snyk as a change agent in helping DevSecOps transformations and it's fine kind of having this capability, but what we really want to get to is this position where developers truly understand and can be better placed to prevent security vulnerabilities being injected into their code. One of the things that is, again, something that's pretty different from the industry from an incumbent perspective is that we believe it's really important to democratize security education. (00:26:06): We have been building this bunch of really high quality but bite size lessons about developer security that focus on developers about security issues and vulnerabilities and we surface them. Again, they're out there in the public domain. There's no paywall to get access to those. All the traditional solutions you need to sign up, you need to pay to get access beyond more than a couple. But these were just, they're all out there in the public domain. That works really well for us from a company generated company distributed loop as well.
turns.zh: 最近一个真有意思的是安全教育。我们把 Snyk 看作推动 DevSecOps 转型的变革者，有这种能力挺好，但我们真正想达到的是这样一种状态：开发者真正理解、并且更有能力防止安全漏洞被写进他们的代码里。其中有一件事， again，从 incumbent 的角度看也和这个行业很不一样——我们坚信，把安全教育民主化非常重要。(00:26:06) 我们一直在构建一批质量很高、但很轻量的开发者安全课程，聚焦开发者关心的安全问题和漏洞，并把它们推出来。同样，它们都在公共领域，获取它们没有任何付费墙。所有传统方案你都得注册、得付费才能看到超过两三个。但我们的这些，全都公开在公共领域。作为“公司生成、公司分发”的闭环，这也非常好用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So cool. SEO and then integrating to GitHub in an interesting way. Imagine there's also a lot of intra-company virality when someone uses Snyk at a company and they spread it to their colleagues?
turns.zh: 太酷了。SEO，再加上用一种有趣的方式集成到 GitHub。我猜当有人在公司里用了 Snyk 并把它传播给同事时，公司内部也会有很多病毒式传播？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, I didn't talk about those. I think those are pretty well understood. We have both referral loops and invite loops as well.
turns.zh: 对，我是说，那些我倒没细说。我觉得那些都很好理解。我们也有推荐闭环和邀请闭环。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, awesome. Coming back to what didn't work, and I think you mentioned that there was a monetization attempt that was self-service oriented and that had some challenges. Can you talk about that?
turns.zh: 好，太棒了。回到那个没奏效的东西，我记得你提到过有一次以自助为导向的变现尝试，遇到了一些挑战。能讲讲吗？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: At the time, a few things were in place. Valuable product, check, strong developer user growth, check, strong retention, check, but the first self-serve monetization efforts only really saw traction with individual developers paying a hundred dollars a month. Or purchases in larger companies, they just didn't happen as everyone had hoped. There was a really critical part of Snyk's history. At the time a bunch of investors didn't lean in, perhaps shy away from early conviction with the founders on building strong usage without a proven path to monetization at that point. Ed at BOLDStart who I mentioned previously, he was one of the first kind of true believers and was I think really key in helping with providing runway during that time. But it was clear that there was a lot of work still to do. The team dived in, they really figured out what the constraints were and through that process really learned about the importance of catering for the broader governance needs of the enterprise buyer. (00:28:07): And that meant a couple of things. First, there was a need to build out table stakes features around governance at scale. Just things that companies of a certain scale and size expected reporting, robust user management and so on. And second that it was time to move beyond that depth first approach, right? That depth first approach was absolutely critical in getting to that point, but it wasn't good enough to take the next step. If you think about it, there's a point in a company scale where you start to see diversification of tech stacks and all of those tech stacks need securing. It's obvious in retrospect that only supporting developers using a narrow slice of those tech stacks wasn't going to meet the needs of the security teams who were ultimately the people who were held accountable for the security of their entire application estate. The teams worked hard over the next few months starting to build support for additional languages and ecosystems and adding those table stakes features. (00:29:04): I think back then Snyk were simply ahead of this inevitable curve of developer first security. At the time, the only buyers were security teams and dev first Security for the most part wasn't something that CISOs and ApSec leaders were driving. But if you look at Snyk through that lens of, as I mentioned, being a change agent, being a key piece of the transformational journey of our customers' DevSecOps journeys, you realize how important it was for us to start to build relationships with those security leaders. It was that time also that it was the right time to bring in the first sales and engineering hires as well.
turns.zh: 当时，好几件事已经就位。有价值的产品，有；强劲的开发者用户增长，有；强留存，有。但最早的自助变现努力，真正看到的 traction，只是个人开发者每月付 100 美元，或者在大公司里的购买根本没像大家期望的那样发生。这是 Snyk 历史上非常关键的一段。当时一批投资人没有加码，也许是当时对创始人在没有成熟变现路径的情况下就建立起强使用量这一点，还缺乏早期的信心。我之前提到的 BOLDStart 的 Ed，是最早的真正信徒之一，我认为他在那段时间为提供 runway 起到了关键作用。但显然还有很多工作要做。团队一头扎了进去，真正搞清楚了约束在哪里，并通过这个过程学到了一件重要的事：要满足企业买家的更广泛治理需求。(00:28:07) 这意味着几件事。第一，需要构建起围绕规模化治理的“桌面筹码”型功能——也就是到了一定规模的公司会期待的东西，比如报表、稳健的用户管理等等。第二，是时候超越那个深度优先的 approach 了，对吧？那个深度优先 approach 在到达那个点上绝对关键，但它不足以支撑下一步。你想想，公司到了一定规模，你会开始看到技术栈的多元化，而所有这些技术栈都需要被保护。回过头看很明显：只支持用技术栈里一小块切片的开发者，是满足不了安全团队的需求的——而安全团队最终才是为整个应用资产的安全性负责的人。团队在接下来的几个月里拼命干，开始为更多语言和生态构建支持，并加上那些“桌面筹码”功能。(00:29:04) 我觉得当年 Snyk 只是走在了“开发者优先的安全”这条必然曲线前面。当时唯一的买家是安全团队，而“开发者优先的安全”在很大程度上还不是 CISO 和应用安全负责人在驱动的东西。但如果你用我提到的那个视角看 Snyk——作为一个变革者，作为客户 DevSecOps 转型旅程里的关键一块——你就会意识到，对我们来说，开始和那些安全负责人建立关系有多重要。也就是在那个时点，也是引入第一批销售和工程招聘的合适时机。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You basically found it couldn't work self-serve, independent of sales being involved in convincing the folks at the top, which makes sense. How do you trust a company with your security if the people at the top responsible for security aren't bought in? Makes sense.
turns.zh: 你基本上发现它没法在脱离销售、去说服高层的情况下自助跑通——这说得通。如果负责安全的高层不买账，你怎么敢把你的安全托付给一家公司？说得通。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Today it's less like that. There are organizations where the buying center is still very much ApSec, but there are also many organizations where kind of technical leaders on the buying decision around security investments. What was always true though even back then was the influencing power of developers, regardless of where the buying center was.
turns.zh: 今天已经不那么像当年了。有些组织里，购买中心仍然是应用安全，但也有很多组织里，技术负责人在关于安全投资的购买决策上有很大话语权。不过即便在当年也一直成立的一点是：开发者的影响力，无论购买中心在哪里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I imagine as the brand has grown, it's gotten easier to convince people like, "Oh yeah, look at all these other logos using this. It's probably going to be okay."
turns.zh: 我猜随着品牌做大，要说服别人就更容易了，比如“看看，这么多别的 logo 都在用这个，那应该问题不大”。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: For sure.
turns.zh: 那当然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to understand in your experience with Snyk, it never really worked self-served monetization. It worked as a way to get into a company and then developers started using it in small scale, but you needed sales and marketing to really grow monetization. Is that what you found?
turns.zh: 我有点想搞清楚，以你在 Snyk 的经验，自助式变现从来没真正跑通过。它作为一种进入一家公司、然后开发者小规模用起来的方式是管用的，但你需要销售和市场才能真正把变现做起来。你发现的是这样吗？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: I think back then, yes. Now it's a very different story. We have a lot of self-serve only customers scaling pretty large, so.
turns.zh: 我觉得在当年，是的。现在故事很不一样了。我们有很多纯自助客户，规模也长得很大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. That's interesting. I rarely hear that you start out with sales being important and it becomes less important or I imagine it's still very important, but there's like a segment that has emerged that can self-serve. Fascinating.
turns.zh: 明白了。这挺有意思。我很少听到一开始销售很重要、后来变得没那么重要的情况——我猜它仍然很重要，但确实出现了一类可以自助的客户群体。真有意思。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Yeah, I think it is important to acknowledge though, that the product has always played a really key part in the sales process for sure.
turns.zh: 对，不过我觉得有一点很重要得承认：产品一直都在销售过程里扮演着非常关键的角色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That touches on something I wanted to ask. [inaudible 00:31:24] you've mentioned him a couple times, he's got this awesome newsletter, he talks about you guys all the time. I think he's very proud of the progress of Snyk and he talks a lot about that for developers, you got to win hearts and minds of developers to build something that works. Any lessons or pieces of advice for folks that are targeting developers to win hearts and minds and get engineers, developers excited about what you're building?
turns.zh: 这就引到了我想问的一件事。[听不清 00:31:24] 你提过他好几次，他有份很棒的 newsletter，老在聊你们。我觉得他挺为 Snyk 的进展骄傲的，也经常说，对开发者来说，你得赢得开发者的心和脑，才能做出真正管用的东西。对于那些以开发者为目标、想赢得工程师和开发者对自己产品在情感上兴奋起来的人，你有什么经验教训或建议吗？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: I think there's two things, right? First of all, fundamentally for someone to get excited about using a product, they've got to care enough, right? They've got to have a problem that you're solving. I think there's two things. One, there is a shift that is happening and still happening. I think there's still a long way to go for developers to really care about security as an integral part of their job in the same way they think about functional quality or performance. I think that we're still, we're making strong progress there. It's changing all the time, but there's still a long way to go there. But the reality is that I think in most companies, developers have to care about security because their companies need to be secure. The key then is how do I make the job of being secure for these developers, as painless as it absolutely needs to be? (00:32:44): And that means really meeting them where they are, integrating with their tools, finding ways to take security to them instead of trying to pull them out of their workflows. Flow is just this incredibly important concept for developers and you want to strive to keep them in that flow for as long as possible. The GitHub kind of pool requests are a great example of that. Someone can sign up for Snyk and they could theoretically be the only user of Snyk and connect their repos. All of a sudden we're protecting, securing those repos, a hundred, a thousand developers could be working in GitHub with that code, all benefiting from Snyk without necessarily needing to sign up. That's that example of taking the product to users without pulling them out of their workflows. I think that's absolutely critical.
turns.zh: 我觉得有两点，对吧？首先，从根本上说，一个人要对用一个产品感到兴奋，他得足够在意，对吧？他得有你在解决的问题。我觉得有两点。其一，一场转变正在发生、而且还在发生。我认为要让开发者真正把安全当作工作中不可分割的一部分、像在乎功能质量或性能那样在乎，还有很长的路要走。我们在这方面进展不错，一直在变，但还差得远。但现实是，我觉得在多数公司里，开发者不得不在意安全，因为他们公司需要安全。那么关键就是：我怎么才能让这些开发者“变得安全”这件事，尽可能不那么痛苦？(00:32:44) 这意味着真的要在他们所在的地方接住他们，和他们的工具集成，想办法把安全送到他们面前，而不是试图把他们从工作流里拽出来。心流对开发者来说是个极其重要的概念，你要尽量让他们尽可能久地待在那个心流里。GitHub 上的 pull request 就是个绝佳例子。有人可以注册 Snyk，理论上他可以是唯一一个用 Snyk 的人，连上他的仓库。突然之间我们就在保护那些仓库了，可能有成百上千的开发者在那个代码上用 GitHub 协作，全都受益于 Snyk，而不一定需要注册。这就是“把产品送到用户面前、而不把他们拽出工作流”的例子。我觉得这绝对关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As an outsider hearing all this, it's a product that magically helps you avoid security issues, very little work, does a lot of the work for you. It's hard to imagine it not working looking at it now, and I'm curious what it was about the early days that just felt like maybe that people didn't believe in this working. Is it just there was doubt that it would be smart enough to find your security vulnerability issues? Was it the timing wasn't right, people weren't ready, weren't concerned about security enough? What do you think it was that created challenges early on? Because looking back, it's like, of course this is going to work. How could it not? It sounds just like a magical all win product.
turns.zh: 作为一个外人听这些，这产品像是魔法一样帮你避开安全问题，几乎不费功夫，还帮你做了一大堆事。现在看很难想象它会不成功，我很好奇：早年到底是什么让人感觉它可能不 work？是因为人们不相信它聪明到能找出你的安全漏洞？还是时机不对、人们没准备好、对安全不够上心？你觉得早年是什么造成了那些挑战？因为回过头看，这当然会成功啊，怎么会不成功呢？听起来就是个魔法般的、全赢的产品。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: First of all, don't think the challenges were there in terms of the developer adoption. Even when those first kind of forays into self-serve were struggling in terms of breaking into some of the larger customers. The developer adoption, the free user base was still growing at a really good pace. That momentum was just constantly building and it's that momentum that has ultimately fueled the sales led business as we've gone through the years. But it was just those few things I think that I mentioned earlier in terms of stumbling blocks that needed to be overcome because when those first sales and marketing hires did join us and we started having conversations and we also tweaked some of the things in the product to meet, had some breadth, had some additional languages, ecosystems, building those table stakes features, then it really unlocked and it was rocket ship time from then.
turns.zh: 首先，我不觉得挑战出在开发者采用上。即便那些最早的自助尝试在打入一些大客户时还在挣扎，开发者的采用、免费用户基数仍然在以很好的速度增长。那股势头一直在累积，而正是这股势头，在这些年里最终推动了我们的销售驱动业务。但就像我之前提到的，是有几件需要克服的绊脚石——因为当那第一批销售和市场招聘进来、我们开始对话、又调了一些产品去满足（有了一些广度、加了一些语言、生态，构建了那些“桌面筹码”功能），然后就真的释放了，从那以后就是火箭升空了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Sounds like the biggest issue is monetization. Can we make money doing this? Developers love it, they're using it like crazy, but will people be convinced to scale this an inside an organization and pay us a bunch of money for it?
turns.zh: 明白了。听起来最大的问题是变现。我们能靠这个赚钱吗？开发者爱它，用得发疯，但人们会被说服在一家组织内部把它规模化、并付我们一大笔钱吗？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Exactly, yep.
turns.zh: 没错，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, got it. I want to dive a little bit deeper into your growth team and product team and how you think about organizing teams like that in a product led growth sales org. The first question, just how did the growth team start at Snyk? What was kind of the early days and then what does it look like today?
turns.zh: 好，明白了。我想稍微深挖一下你的增长团队和产品团队，以及你怎么思考在一家产品驱动增长（又带销售）的组织里，去搭建这样的团队。第一个问题，Snyk 的增长团队最开始是怎么起来的？早期是什么样，现在又是什么样？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: There were some ad hoc efforts happening in various places. We had a small growth marketing function, we had [inaudible 00:35:49]. We also had some ownership of key growth services in R&D. There was a team that owned the new user onboarding flows, for example. But it wasn't until I joined that we really formalized the notion of a growth team. It was very kind of ad hoc before then. When I joined, we created what we call the developer growth group now. Before then there maybe wasn't strong an understanding about what a growth team needs to look like, how they might need to work differently to the core product teams. And I'd say overall it was much later than you'd typically expect to see. And at a bigger scale. You normally are going to start growth teams, one or two people, three or four maybe, and scale out from there. But we started much bigger than that. But at the same time, this bottom up developer first approach, it was baked into the company DNA in terms of how teams think and operate. Yeah, we were growing fast even before we spun up the growth group. I think the significant change that happened there, it was a transition from a simple freemium approach to a holistic and well-coordinated PLG strategy. It's much more common to start earlier, much more common to start at a smaller scale than we did at Snyk, but it worked for us because of this kind of perfect storm of where we had a product with that bottom up growth built in from the beginning. We had founders with a deep appreciation for how the product could grow and there was strongly exec alignment and sponsorship for scaling the motion. The problem when starting the growth group, it was really for the most part more oriented to how we can get the flywheel spinning faster as opposed to getting it moving in the first place.

(00:51:14): I don't know if it's too far off track here, but I have a vision and mission framework that I like to use that leads to I think, great simple statements of an imagined better future state and your role in getting there. So I can talk about that a little bit if it's a-
turns.zh: 这是个大话题。基于我看到的奏效和不那么奏效的，我有很多想法。我想大致能归成三个主要主题。第一是人和流程，第二是策略，第三是数据。它们都相关，而且都得运作良好，增长才有效。先从人说起，就刚才说的均衡团队那第一点——你得有那些在多样性和产生好点子能力上均衡、同时也有执行力的团队。所以这是第一件事。(00:47:14) 但还是说人的话题，我有个心智模型：潜力在核心上是无限的，但很多情境性的东西阻止人们发挥潜力。可能是他思考某事的方式，可能是组织性的，可能是和同事的关系或更广的团队动态，甚至可能他根本没在合适的角色上。(00:47:37) 所以根本上，我认为管理者和领导者的角色，是帮他们识别这些事，并和他们一起找到茁壮生长和成长的方式。我在一个增长组织里尤其看到这点的重要性——那里的人天然就更不那么 fit。这不代表他们不是有才华的牛人，只是说他们在增长的语境里做不出最好的工作。(00:47:59) 所以当你起步一个增长团队时，你常常靠内部调动来组建。这比外部候选人更容易被忽略——外部候选人在招聘时你很可能会显式地测这些事。我拿开发者举个例子。(00:48:17) 在增长语境里真正茁䊨的开发者，是那些被“快速行动、迭代以创造可衡量影响”驱动的人。他们不执着于自己的作品。他们把不完美当作过程的一部分来拥抱。他们乐意丢弃自己的代码、甚至自己的想法。他们好奇，总在找方法更接近用户。(00:48:38) 那些通常就是很棒的增长工程师；而我也认识一些不可思议的工程师，他们在攻克很深的技术挑战、热爱过程不亚于热爱结果时最有动力，他们在增长里就很挣扎。当然现实永远没那么简单，没有人真的在光谱的任何一端。但试着回答“这个人能在这个环境里做出最好的工作吗”真的很重要。所以我觉得这是很关键的一部分。(00:49:10) 而且，你也需要确保他们从技能和知识角度装备妥当。所以他们需要有对的技能和知识，才能在你增长流程的语境里做出最好的工作。理想状态是：每个增长团队成员有共同词汇，他们对增长流程感到舒服，能很好地和数据与实验平台协作，他们理解数据，有对的技能和心态。(00:49:36) 教育我认为在这里起很大作用。所以我们是 Reforge 的忠实粉丝，但也开发了一批内部项目来对齐和提升团队。我们学到的一课，比如：从简单起步、等团队积累经验再加深，很重要。所以比如，说到实验，别一上来就引入多变量测试或者序贯抽样、替代评估方法这类概念。(00:50:04) 团队还在试着把脚趾探进那片水，这简直是犯一堆错的配方。所以这是一点建议。(00:50:15) 但人也需要对齐。我其实在最近做的另一档播客上聊过这个。我意思是：他们的执行需要对齐一个演进中的增长策略；增长策略需要对齐、同时影响公司往哪去；增长策略需要钩住产品策略，理想情况下 KPI 有一些重叠和对齐，这样增长团队和核心产品团队朝同一个方向游。团队的技能和经验和策略要对齐。如果你得聚焦激活和获取，那一个定价套餐专家在那时大概就不是对的技能组合。(00:50:57) 但你作为领导者也要规划好，确保随着增长团队焦点不可避免地随时间转移，那些技能是可得的。但说到底，我觉得每个人都得能轻松回答“我为什么在这”这个问题——他们做的工作为什么重要。(00:51:14) 不知道是不是偏太远了，但我有个挺喜欢的愿景和使命框架，能导出我认为很棒的、简洁的关于“想象中更好的未来状态”和“你在抵达那里的角色”的陈述。如果你愿意我可以稍微讲讲——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, let's do it. That sounds too good to pass up.
turns.zh: 好啊，讲吧。这听起来好到不能错过。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: -Cool. So the vision is the nirvana state that you aim to enable for your users and customers in five to 10 years. It's something that could equally be enabled by your competitors if you don't execute effectively or efficiently or quickly enough. You can always prefix a vision statement with in the future, dot, dot dot. (00:51:52): Now it's something that should be bound to your target market. So not too wide and not too narrow. And critically it should not mention your company, your product, or anything solution related at all. Completely agnostic of those things. (00:52:05): And then the mission, that's the thing that you are going to relentlessly iterate on to take you incrementally closer to the nirvana state described in the vision. It should answer how you'll realize the vision by describing what your fundamental approach will be. In other words, what you will do and how you'll do it. It should ideally aim to encode any unique differentiating advantage you have. So if I think about Snyk at large when it comes to advantage, we might mention our unequal security intelligence and knowledge of application context. (00:52:36): And one of the neat things about this framework is if you find utility in doing so, you can apply it at every level from the company level all the way down to individual team. It doesn't mean the process is not difficult and you need to spend a lot of time, but it gives you this set of kind of a framework, a set of bounds that help you really come out with world crafted statements that kind of stand the test of time.
turns.zh: ——酷。愿景，是你旨在为用户和客户在 5 到 10 年里促成的“涅槃状态”。它也可能被你的竞争对手促成，如果你执行得不够有效、不够高效、不够快。你总可以在愿景陈述前加“在未来，……”。(00:51:52) 它应该绑定你的目标市场，所以别太宽也别太窄。关键点是，它完全不该提到你的公司、你的产品、或任何和解决方案相关的东西。对那些东西完全中立。(00:52:05) 然后是使命，那是你将无情迭代、带你逐步接近愿景里描述的涅槃状态的东西。它应该回答“你怎么通过描述你的根本 approach 来实现愿景”。换句话说，你要做什么、以及你怎么去做。它理想情况下要编码进你任何独特的差异化优势。所以如果我泛泛想 Snyk 的优势，我们也许会提到我们无与伦比的安全情报和对应用上下文的认知。(00:52:36) 这个框架一个巧妙之处是：如果你觉得有用，它可以用在从公司层级一直往下到单个团队的每一层。这不意味着过程不困难、你不需要花很多时间，但它给你一套框架、一套边界，帮你真正写出能经受时间考验的、精心打磨的陈述。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example you could share of the mission vision, whether it's Snyk or something else?
turns.zh: 你能否分享一个使命愿景的例子，不管是 Snyk 的还是别的？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. I'll give you one for the growth group of Snyk. So great. The vision, every developer securely unleashes their creativity and the mission is to connect every developer and their organizations to the value of the Snyk platform with frictionless self-serve, adoption and expansion.
turns.zh: 可以，可以。我给你一个 Snyk 增长组的。愿景：每一位开发者都能安全地释放他们的创造力。使命：通过无摩擦的自助采用和扩张，把每一位开发者及其组织连接到 Snyk 平台的价值上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting how the vision is so big beyond Snyk's current focus. And to your point, this kind of trickle down, right? There's a company vision and mission and it's the growth team's mission vision.
turns.zh: 有意思，愿景大到超出了 Snyk 当前的焦点。就像你说的，这种涓滴而下，对吧？有公司的愿景和使命，也有增长团队的使命愿景。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to shift a bit and talk about your product work. So we've talked a lot about the growth org. I'm curious what the broader product org looks like. How many teams do you have? How do you structure it? Is it like product focused, user focused, outcome focused? And then just how does that team work with the growth team?
turns.zh: 我想转一下，聊聊你的产品工作。我们聊了很多增长组织。我好奇更广义的产品组织长什么样。你有几个团队？你怎么搭结构？是产品聚焦、用户聚焦、还是结果聚焦？然后那个团队怎么和增长团队协作？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Sure. Happy to go into a bunch of that stuff. I know I'd mentioned earlier kind of three areas of building a growth team. I don't know if you want me to cover those other two. 'Cause we talked about-
turns.zh: 当然。很高兴聊那些。我记得早先提到过搭建增长团队三个领域。不知道你想不想让我把另两个也覆盖？因为我们聊了——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh yeah, okay, let's do that. Let's finish that thread.
turns.zh: 哦对，好，那就做这个。把那条线收完。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: -Cool. So people and process was the first and we'll cover process really quickly. I think on the process side, at a minimum here you need well understood, documented growth processes, practices, working cadences. Teams in growth need to work differently in some ways from R and D teams working on core product, assuming otherwise, and just giving growth responsibility to an existing team without working with them to implement appropriate ways of working. I think it's a common track. (00:54:31): Ideally you get to a point there where the growth process is something that's continually refined and iterated on trying to build in more predictability. But what I've found I think most singularly most important in a growth process is facilitating a rapid learning cadence and providing the means to socialize those learnings, surfacing them in the right place at the right time so they can be leveraged and at the context. And if you think about experimentation, it's not about delivering outcomes it's about generating learnings that the organization can leverage effectively to deliver outcomes. (00:55:05): Might not be now, might not be tomorrow or some point in the future. But the sad reality is that without good process learnings easily end up unused and gathering dust. And you have to ask then what was the point? So as people in process and you know when that's on the right track, when you start to see enthusiastic sharing of learnings, when you see regular contribution of ideas coming from everyone in the form of well crafted hypotheses that are based on data and learnings. And when you see a wide variety of folks, just assuming end to end ownership of managing and running experiments instead of delegating that to the product manager or an engineer and tech lead. So yeah, that's people in process and strategy is-
turns.zh: ——酷。所以人和流程是第一块，我们很快聊完流程。我觉得在流程这边，你至少需要有被大家理解、被记录下来的增长流程、实践和工作节奏。增长团队在某些方面需要和以不同方式工作，区别于做核心产品的研发团队——假设不是这样，只是把增长职责丢给一个现有团队、而不和他们一起落地合适的工作方式，我觉得这是个常见陷阱。(00:54:31) 理想情况下你达到一个点：增长流程是被持续打磨、迭代的，试图建立起更多可预测性。但我在增长流程里发现最重要的一件事，是促进一种快速学习的节奏，并提供把那些学习“社会化”出去的手段——在合适的时机、合适的地点把它们浮现出来，好让它们能在对的语境下被利用。如果你想想实验，它的目的不是交付结果，而是产生组织能有效利用、从而交付结果的学习。(00:55:05) 也许不是现在，也许不是明天，是将来某个点。但悲哀的现实是：没有好的流程，学习很容易就根本没被用上、积了灰。那你得问，那还有什么意义？所以当人和流程走上正轨时，你会看到人们热情地分享学习，看到每个人以基于数据和学习的、精心打磨的假设形式持续贡献点子，看到各种各样的人直接端到端地拥有并运行实验，而不是把那委派给产品经理或工程师和技术负责人。所以，这就是人和流程，而策略是——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me throw in a question real quick before we get to the last piece.
turns.zh: 在说到最后一块之前，我先快速插一个问题。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So learnings, just to kind of touch on that. I've heard more and more pushback on the idea of learnings being an outcome. Because a lot of... As a leader, you're not going to be like, Cool, we learned so many things but nothing really got done. How do you think about the tension between, yeah, learnings we want to learn, but we also want to move metrics, grow the business and learnings are a way to inform decisions more than even just learn. How do you think about that kind of balance?
turns.zh: 关于学习，稍微碰一下。我听到越来越多对“学习作为一个产出”这个想法的反弹。因为很多……作为领导者，你不会说“酷，我们学到了这么多东西但什么都没真做出来”。你怎么看待这种张力：对，我们想学习，但我们也想推动指标、增长业务，而学习更多是 informing 决策，而不只是学习本身。你怎么看这种平衡？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Ultimately you're there to create impact, right? There's no getting away from that, but learnings is the means. It's the same as, there's a quote that I love from [inaudible 00:56:27] around focus on the user's path to value not on monetization. Because if you focus on the form of the latter will follow, and that's the same thing with learnings and impact here. If you try and focus on the impact itself might struggle. If you focus on the things you need in terms of learnings to take you step by step, that will pave the path to creating impact.
turns.zh: 说到底你是为了创造影响，对吧？这个逃不掉，但学习是手段。这就像我很喜欢的一句[听不清 00:56:27]的话：“聚焦用户通往价值的路径，而不是聚焦变现。因为如果你聚焦前者，后者自然会来。”学习和影响在这里也是一回事。如果你试图直接聚焦影响本身，你可能会挣扎。如果你聚焦你在学习上需要的东西、带你一步步走，那会铺出创造影响的路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine your OKRs and goals are still like move this metrics some percentage, but you think of that as an output and the input is let's learn a bunch of stuff about what works and doesn't work and use that to inform what we're going to double down on.
turns.zh: 我猜你的 OKR 和目标还是像“把这个指标挪动某个百分比”，但你认为那是产出，而输入是“我们来学一大堆什么管用、什么不管用，并用它来 inform 我们要加倍下注什么”。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Exactly. Yeah.
turns.zh: 没错。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. Okay.
turns.zh: 好。可以。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: You got to focus on when you build a strategic opportunity, you are thinking about the outcomes, but you don't just go right to the end state. You've got to think about what's the quickest way we can test this hypothesis? And from there, what we learn from that and what do we take into the next set of the next set of experiments and it... You're paving this path along the way. You kind of that rough destination. How you get there, you don't know at the start. And that's what the path that the learnings take you on.
turns.zh: 当你构建一个战略机会时，你得聚焦在结果上，但你不是直接跳到终态。你得想：我们能用最快的方式测试这个假设是什么？从那里，我们学到什么，又把它带进下一组实验——你是在沿路铺这条路。你大概知道个粗糙的目的地。怎么到那，你一开始不知道。而那就是学习带你走的路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. Okay. And then strategy we're talking about.
turns.zh: 酷。好。然后我们聊策略。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Strategy. Yeah, so strategy, it's a good one. At a very basic level, you need to be able to answer questions. How do you acquire users? How do you retain users? How do you monetize them? I know you talked with Elena on that in more depth, but from there you need more detail. It's going to guide the growth teams and where they look for strategic opportunity, how they approach that. The best way I've found to articulate a growth strategy that fulfills the promise of usefully guiding the team's execution, it's the loop based model, Reforge, as specific kind of documentation that I think is great around that. (00:58:15): Being able to identify the various micro and macro loops, how they're all connected, being able to document them in a qualitative model to communicate a shared understanding of how you grow. It's really powerful. Augmenting that then with the quantitative side of things, that helps guide quarter to quarter focus and ensure you can be intentional about where you're investing. That becomes a big enabler. (00:58:40): You're never going to have a shortage of ideas in a high performing growth team. So knowing where to focus amidst that kind of sea of ideas is a really important role of the strategy and fairly on, you'll probably have one or two core loops, but inevitably you'll need to layer on and connect new ones over time. And having a framework for doing that and having a framework for regularly revisiting that in the context of growth, team learnings, changes in broader company strategy, evolution of the product, new features being added, and so on. Market shifts, that becomes a big up level for teams to be able to create timely impact. (00:59:19): So the model you create there is what enables you to know at any time where the biggest constraints to your growth are and allows you to balance your growth investments accordingly. It's neat for sure. We've had times where we've focused on a broad set of constraints and opportunities and other times where we've had a much narrower focus. For example, on driving improvement to activation and engagement, even more narrowed like doing that through empty states, for example.
turns.zh: 策略。对，策略，这是个好话题。在最基础的层面，你需要能回答一些问题。你怎么获取用户？你怎么留住用户？你怎么从他们身上变现？我知道你和 Elena 在那块聊得更深，但从那之后你需要更多细节。它会指导增长团队、以及他们去哪找战略机会、怎么 approach 那个。我发现能把“有用指导团队执行”这个承诺兑现的增长策略表述方式，是基于闭环的模型——Reforge 有关于那个的具体文档，我觉得很棒。(00:58:15) 能够识别出各种微观和宏观闭环，理解它们如何相互关联，并能够把它们记录在一个定性模型里，来传递一种关于“你怎么增长”的共识性理解，这真的很有力量。再叠加定量的部分，它帮助指导一个季度到一个季度的重点，确保你能有意识地把资源投在哪——这就成了一个巨大的推动力。(00:58:40) 在一个高效增长团队里你永远不缺想法。所以，在那样一片想法海洋里知道聚焦在哪，是策略一个非常重要的角色。而且，你大概会有一两个核心闭环，但不可避免地，随时间你需要叠加上新的、并把它们连起来。而有一个做这件事的框架，以及一个在增长、团队学习、更广的公司策略变化、产品演进、新功能加入等等语境里定期重访它的框架——市场变化——那对团队能创造及时的影響，是个很大的提升。(00:59:19) 所以你在那创建的模型，能让你随时知道增长最大的约束在哪，并让你相应地平衡增长投资。当然很妙。我们有时候聚焦在一组较宽的约束和机会上，有时候聚焦窄得多——比如，驱动激活和互动的改善，甚至更窄，比如通过空状态来做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to unpack the strategy piece real quick. How do you operationalize this idea of you have this growth model, growth loop, you figured out here's the ways we're growing. How do you tactically connect that to a strategy? Is it, here's how we're growing, here's where we're going to focus this quarter, optimize this part of the loop, or is there some other way? You write it down, basically.
turns.zh: 我想快速拆一下策略这块。你是怎么把这个“你有个增长模型、增长闭环，你搞清楚了我们是怎么增长的”的想法 operationalize 成策略的？是“这是我们在怎么增长，这是本季度我们要聚焦的、要优化闭环的这一块”，还是有别的方式？基本上你把它写下来。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Very simply, it's first of all alignment on how you grow the different loops, how they work, the roles of different teams and the roles that they play in fueling those loops and getting them to spin faster. I think that's the first thing, having that common vocabulary and understanding. (01:00:25): Second is understanding the way they work in terms of what is constraining them, what are the inputs to them? What are the opportunities for making those loops spin faster? How can multiple loops work together in a macro context? (01:00:41): And particularly using the data there to be able to identify and understand and get alignment around where are the biggest constraints in your growth model overall and therefore where are the things that we need to focus on as a team over the next quarter or two quarters, and so on. (01:01:01): And that it's constantly changing. As I mentioned, there's a bunch of stuff that needs to feed back into that model in terms of growth loop performance or the learnings you're making and so on. That means it's changing and you're constantly reevaluating and it's guiding kind of quarter to quarter planning.
turns.zh: 很简单，首先是共识：你是怎么增长的不同闭环、它们怎么运作、不同团队的角色、以及它们在给那些闭环供能并让它们转得更快上扮演的角色。我觉得这是第一件事，有那个共同词汇和理解。(01:00:25) 第二是理解它们运作的方式——什么在约束它们，它们的输入是什么，让那些闭环转得更快的机会在哪，多个闭环怎么在宏观语境里一起工作。(01:00:41) 尤其是用那里的数据，去识别、理解、并就“你的增长模型整体上最大的约束在哪、因此接下来一两个季度我们需要聚焦的东西在哪”达成共识。(01:01:01) 而且它在持续变化。就像我说的，有一大堆东西需要反馈进那个模型——闭环表现、你做出的学习等等。这意味着它在变，你在持续重估，它在指导一个季度到一个季度的规划。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. So just to make it even more concrete for folks that are listening. So one of your loops is this integration with GitHub where you automatically fix their code and create a PR. You may find at some point somebody clicking that link to becoming a user is too high friction, too many people are falling out. So one strategy for one of say the activation team could be we're going to optimize this part of the funnel. So when clicking from GitHub to sign up as a user and get them to a point where they found value, right?
turns.zh: 酷。为了让听的人更具体一点。你的一个闭环是和 GitHub 的集成——你自动修他们的代码、创建一个 PR。你可能在某个点发现，有人点那个链接变成用户摩擦太高，太多人掉出去了。所以其中一个团队——比如激活团队——的一个策略可以是：我们要优化漏斗的这一块。也就是从点 GitHub 到注册成用户、并让他们到达找到价值的点，对吧？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Yep. That exactly that sort of thing. Or earlier on, for example, it might have been with that taken that same example of that same loop, and this is sufficiently far in the past that it's easy for me to talk about. But we start with GitHub. We want to now expand the scope of that loop. We've seen success with it. We see the performance of that loop growing, but we think there's opportunity in saying let's expand that by adding support for Bitbucket. And now all of a sudden we spin up that same loop with Bitbucket and then GitLab and so on.
turns.zh: 对。就是那种事。或者更早，用同一个闭环的例子——这已经够久远了，所以我好讲。我们从 GitHub 开始。我们想现在扩那个闭环的范围。我们看到了成功。我们看到那个闭环的表现在增长，但我们认为机会在于：通过加对 Bitbucket 的支持来扩展它。然后突然之间，我们在 Bitbucket 上、接着 GitLab 等等，启动了同一个闭环。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. We could go a whole hour on just that piece, so we'll move on and we'll save that for feed two.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好。光那一块我们就能聊一整个小时，所以继续，留到第二期。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Data was the last thing. And growth team just can't function without data that even with early stage products, before you have the needed volume of traffic to be able to run formal tests in reasonable timeframes, you still need to have signals that help you learn and inform your decisions, both quantum and of course qu through speaking with users. My advice there is really just to invest early the infrastructure, the tooling then at a given scale, the dedicated people as well. They're going to be core to building out the growth team and they'll enable data to ultimately pretty much inform all critical decisions. (01:03:01): So Snyk was interesting that we didn't have a problem of not having enough data. In fact, there was an abundance of data, like too much. We collected absolutely everything. And the problem I identified very early was that we didn't have enough behavioral specific data and we weren't intentional enough about the data that we were collecting and how we were collecting it, which made the data hard to trust and that becomes a big problem. (01:03:26): So we invested in tooling and processes for building out event tracking plans, and now we test conformance to schema of the instrumented code in our CI processes. So we have absolute confidence in the data. So that was getting to a point of trustworthy behavioral data was absolutely key. (01:03:43): But the reason I say invest early here is that to remember that it also takes time to accrue enough data that you can learn about and make some key decisions around retention, for example. Also that you have enough data to run regressions on, be able to inform definition of your activation metrics or engagement states and so on. So the earlier you can start collecting the better. So yeah, people in process a strategy and data and you absolutely need all of those things to build and run an affected growth team. (01:04:14): When you get all of those things working, it's like rocket fuel for focus creativity, but at the same time slowing down to put the maturity in place as on all scales at the pace Snyk has it's pretty much impossible. You still have to get stuff done while you're kind of building all that stuff out. You have to accept that you're going to make a bunch of mistakes along the way. You have to be a hundred percent comfortable with that. And you have to treat those mistakes as learning opportunities that provide leaves for improvement. (01:04:43): And it's also useful to... You know, asked about KPIs and what the team are responsible for it. And that is one way in which a growth team absolutely needs to make impact and it's the way that primarily they're going to be held accountable. But it's also I think, useful to think about the efficacy of the growth org, not just in terms of the impact they drive our experiments and new product experiences and on core growth pick KPIs, but also how they enable and uplevel the rest of the org. (01:05:10): So for example, our entire product led sales process, it's powered by an evolving model that describes our understanding of users, teams, accounts, the usage and adoption patterns and signals, the best in form where and how our GTM teams focused. Insights from growth teams often have utility far beyond growth, but people can't know if something is useful to them if you haven't shared it with them. So the learnings made in the growth teams, even those from mistakes or failures, we socialize them widely and visibly. (01:05:41): We want every R and D team to be leveraging experimentation where appropriate to learn to create business impact. So one of the things we did here is creating a paved row for adoption of behavioral analytics and experimentation stack, coach teams on getting started to make it as easy as possible for anyone to start to reap the benefits of the platform, built out internal education programs on data driven development, on experimentation, built internal tools to help with metrics design and so on. (01:06:08): And then building core platform services as well that are useful for people outside of growth. So we built services that power contextual onboarding, and originally that was the intent, but now those same services can be used anywhere in the product to give contextual experiences. I know that was a bit of a ramble, but hopefully there's one or two useful things in there.
turns.zh: 数据是最后一块。没有数据，增长团队根本没法运转——即使早期产品，在你还没有足够流量能在合理时间框架里跑正式测试时，你仍然需要有信号帮你学习、informing 决策，无论是量化的，还是当然通过对用户说话获得的质的。我那里的建议就是尽早投资基础设施、工具，然后在某个规模上，也投资专人。它们对搭建增长团队是核心，会让数据最终基本上 inform 所有关键决策。(01:03:01) 所以 Snyk 有趣的一点是，我们不存在数据不够的问题。事实上，数据多到泛滥。我们什么都收集。而我很早就发现的问题是：我们没有足够具体的行为数据，而且对我们收集什么数据、怎么收集，不够有意识，这导致数据难被信任，而那成了个大问题。(01:03:26) 所以我们投资了工具和方法，去构建事件追踪计划，现在我们还在 CI 流程里测试埋点代码对 schema 的符合度。所以我们对数据有绝对的信心。所以，达到“可信的行为数据”那一点，绝对关键。(01:03:43) 但我之所以说早投资，是因为要记住：积累到足够让你能学习、并围绕留存做关键决策的数据，也需要时间。同样，你要有足够数据去跑回归、去 inform 你的激活指标或互动状态的定义等等。所以你越早开始收集越好。所以，人、流程、策略、数据——你绝对需要所有这些来搭建并运行一个有效的增长团队。(01:04:14) 当你把所有这些都跑起来，它就像聚焦创造力的火箭燃料，但同时，要在 Snyk 这种速度下把所有成熟度都就位，基本不可能。你仍然得在搭建所有这些的同时把事做出来。你必须接受一路上你会犯一堆错。你必须百分之百对此舒服。而且你必须把那些错误当成改进的学习机会。(01:04:43) 还有一点有用……你问过 KPI 和团队负责什么。那是一个增长团队绝对需要创造影响的维度，也是他们主要被问责的方式。但我认为，有用的是把增长组织的效能，不只看成他们在实验和新产品体验上、在核心增长 KPI 上驱动的影响，也看成他们怎么赋能并提升组织其余部分。(01:05:10) 比如，我们整个产品驱动销售流程，是由一个演进中的模型驱动的——那个模型描述我们对用户、团队、账户、使用和采用模式与信号的理解，以及我们的 GTM 团队最好把精力放在哪、怎么放。增长团队的洞察常常有用到远超增长本身，但如果没分享给别人，人们不会知道某样东西对他们有用。所以增长团队做出的学习，即使是那些来自错误或失败的，我们也广泛且可见地社会化它们。(01:05:41) 我们希望每个研发团队都恰当地利用实验，去创造业务影响。所以我们这里做的一件事，是给行为分析和实验栈的采用铺一条“ paving road（铺好的路）”，指导团队上手，让任何人尽可能容易地开始收获平台的好处；构建了关于数据驱动开发、关于实验的内部教育项目；构建了帮做指标设计的内部工具等等。(01:06:08) 然后也构建了核心平台服务，对增长之外的人也有用。我们构建了驱动“情境化 onboarding”的服务，原本意图是这个，但现在同样的服务能在产品任何地方用来给情境化体验。我知道有点啰嗦，但希望里面有那么一两件有用的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, there's two things I wanted to quickly follow up and then we can talk about the product team. You said you socialize learnings and experiment results. Is there anything you could share there about tips to do that? You have a tool you do use that for? Is there someone posts stuff in Slack? Is it an email that goes out? How do you actually socialize learning such that say a salesperson can do something with it?
turns.zh: 对，有两件事我想快速追问，然后我们聊产品团队。你说你把学习和实验结果社会化。那里有什么能分享的 tips 吗？你用一个工具来做这个？是有人在 Slack 里发东西？是一封发出去的邮件？你到底怎么把学习社会化，好让比如一个销售能用它做点什么？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Yes. So there's, first of all, there's a bunch of Slack channels like Synk runs on Slack basically. So there's a bunch of Slack channels. Even when we're planning experiments, those are kind of wide and in the open and we invite collaboration on those. But from a ceremony perspective, we try hard to institutionalize ways to generate and leverage learnings. It's something I feel pretty strongly about. So we have these team level impact and learnings reviews loosely modeled from a blog years back down, I don't know... Six years I want to say that Brian Balfour wrote about a similar ceremony from these HubSpot days. (01:07:26): And if I had to pick one meeting that as the most important in the growth team, it would be this. The teams continuously document any learnings from data exploration, from experimentation, from user research and so on. They document that in their weekly impact and learnings document. (01:07:43): Some teams find it better to pair up and advanced into dedicated learning sessions to deep dive on specific relevant topics. But however it comes together, it's all put into that document. (01:07:53): When it comes to the meeting itself, it's usually run by the pm. Most of it is spent discussing learnings that have been documented, their implications, how they can be leveraged in follow up work, where they might have relevance to other teams and so on. For relatively smaller part of the meeting is also spent looking at key metrics. Some teams have actually split that out entirely into a separate meeting. And then no time at all is spent reviewing what the team have actually been doing. It's more on kind of the outcomes and the learning. So that's at the team level. (01:08:21): But then we run that same meeting at the group level on a monthly basis. So that's run by the product engineering or marketing director for the growth group. And that's where all of the growth teams come together. They share some key learnings, can't share everything. Of course, what they're doing is picking specific learnings that have potential relevance in utility across the other teams. So also as a standing agenda item for our user research team to share what we call developer insights. That's one of my personal favorite meetings to attend. It's always recorded and socialize with the rest of the company afterwards. And yeah, I'd say that's really important, but there's a bunch of different ways in which we're filing out that information constantly.
turns.zh: 有。首先，有一堆 Slack 频道——Snyk 基本跑在 Slack 上。所以有各种 Slack 频道。甚至我们在规划实验时，那些也是宽开的、公开的，我们邀请协作。但从仪式角度，我们很努力地把“产生并利用学习”的方式制度化。这点我挺强烈的。我们有这些团队级的“影响和学习的复盘”，松散地借鉴了好些年前——我想说是六年前——Brian Balfour 写的一篇关于 HubSpot 年代类似仪式的博客。(01:07:26) 如果要我挑增长团队里最重要的一个会议，就是它。团队持续记录来自数据探索、实验、用户研究等等的学习。他们把那记录在每周的“影响和学习”文档里。(01:07:43) 有些团队觉得两两配对、进阶到专门的学习会、就具体相关主题深潜更好。但无论怎么组合，都放进那个文档。(01:07:53) 说到会议本身，通常由 PM 主持。大部分时间花在讨论已记录的学习、它们的含义、怎么在后续工作里被利用、它们可能在哪对别的团队有相关性等等。会议相对较小的一部分也花在看关键指标上。有些团队其实把那完全拆成了另一个会议。而完全不花时间复盘团队实际在做什么。更多是结果和学习。所以那是团队级。(01:08:21) 然后我们在组级也跑同一个会议，每月一次。那由增长组的产品、工程或市场总监主持。所有增长团队聚到一起。他们分享一些关键学习，不可能什么都分享。当然，他们做的是挑那些对其他团队有潜在相关性和用处的特定学习。所以也作为我们用户研究团队的固定议程项，来分享我们叫“开发者洞察”的东西。那是我个人最爱参加的会议之一。它总是被录下来，事后在公司其余部分社会化。对，我觉得那真的很重要，但我们有各种各样的方式在持续地“填出”那些信息。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So cool. And this is a meeting that anyone can come to like a sales person comes to. PART 3 OF 4 ENDS [01:09:04]
turns.zh: 太酷了。这是个谁都能来的会议，比如一个销售也会来。[01:09:04] 第 3 段 / 共 4 段 结束

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this is a meeting that anyone can come to like a sales person comes to see what interesting stuff the product team has learned recently from experiments. How cool. Would you be able to share a template of that document that you put together that we could include in the show notes?
turns.zh: 这是个谁都能来的会议，比如一个销售会来，看看产品团队最近从实验里学到了什么有趣的东西。多酷。你能分享一份你们整理的那份文档的模板、好让我们放进 show notes 吗？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Yeah, for sure.
turns.zh: 当然，可以。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. And then the meeting, you said it's run by basically like some of the product functions and ideas to share things they've learned in recent experiments, say in the past month.
turns.zh: 好。那会议，你说基本是由一些产品职能主持，大家分享他们最近实验里学到的东西，比如过去一个月。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: So typically the team level ceremony, it's PM-led. That's from more from a facilitation perspective. The learnings are all brought forward by the various folks in the team and each one of them who's contributed to learning will talk about that learning with the group and facilitate the discussion from there. And then at the group level, those are read by the directors for the growth group and each team it might be an engineering lead, it might be a tech lead, it might be a designer, it might be the product manager. We'll talk about some key learnings from that month.
turns.zh: 通常团队级的仪式是 PM 主导的，更多是 facilitation 视角。学习全由团队里各个人带来，每个贡献了学习的人会和小组成员讲那个学习，并从那 facilitation 讨论。然后在组级，那些由增长组的总监们读，每个团队可能是工程负责人、技术负责人、设计师或产品经理。我们会讲那个月的一些关键学习。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Makes sense. If there's nothing PMs are good at, it's facilitating meetings. So that makes sense. Okay. And so that's a good segue to just chatting a bit about the product org. I'm curious just like how you structure the product team and then how that works with the growth team.
turns.zh: 有道理。如果 PM 有什么擅长的，那就是主持会议。所以说得通。好。那很好地引到了聊聊产品组织。我好奇你怎么搭产品团队，然后它怎么和增长团队协作。

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: That's good. So the product org, what do you want to know?
turns.zh: 好。产品组织，你想知道什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Broadly, how do you structure it? Just like how many teams do you have? Do you align it across by outcome or is it by surface area of a product? And then is the growth team like adjacent to this product org? Is it like a unit within the product org or is it integrated? But I don't think it is. So what does that look like org chart wise?
turns.zh: 广义上，你怎么搭结构？比如你有几个团队？你是按结果对齐，还是按产品的某个面（surface area）？然后增长团队是和产品组织相邻吗？是产品组织里的一个单元，还是集成的？但我觉得不是。那在组织图上长什么样？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: I think we've got a fairly common pattern for how we structure our product and wider R&D org. So most of the org functional ownership-based, there are a lot of really complex domains in the core product. So having that localized knowledge is important to be able to own and run the code that teams ship. The growth teams, on the other hand, are structured by outcomes. We talked about that already. Owning areas like acquisition, activation, engagement, monetization. These outcomes and team remits change over time as we talked about. But the teams here are often working on areas of the product where they don't own the code, which I think is the key difference between how we structure our growth teams and product teams with some exceptions. One of the growth teams actually own the onboarding flows and so on. So that does require a lot of trust. (01:11:25): It requires very transparent communication mechanisms built into how we work. One of the meetings that we have regularly is experiment plan reviews. They're ad hoc meetings. They're led by the experiment lead, could be the PM, could be anyone else in the team. But the important thing is a bunch of people will be invited there, especially stakeholders from other teams where we might be experimenting on their surfaces and that won't be the first time they've learned about this. We'd like to try and actually include them in co-designing the experiment plan so they're fully on board with it. But absolutely kind of inviting them into those experiment and views really key. If we're going to run an experiment on that surface, we need to make sure that everything in that experiment plan is watertight, especially from a scheduling perspective because the last thing we want is a week and a half into an experiment for some change to happen within that surface from the product team unaware that an experiment's happening and completely invalidate the experiment.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们产品和更广研发组织的结构，是个相当常见的模式。所以组织大部分是基于职能所有权的，核心产品里有很多真的很复杂的领域。所以拥有局域化知识，对拥有并运行团队发布的代码很重要。另一方面，增长团队是按结果组织的。我们聊过那个。拥有像获取、激活、互动、变现这样的领域。这些结果和团队职责随时间变化，就像我们聊的。但这里的团队常常在做他们不拥有代码的产品的某些区域——我觉得这是我们的增长团队和产品团队结构的关键区别，有少数例外。其中一个增长团队其实拥有 onboarding 流程等等。所以那确实需要很多信任。(01:11:25) 它需要在我们工作的方式里内建非常透明的沟通机制。我们有一个定期的会议叫“实验计划评审”。它们是临时的会议。由实验负责人主持，可能是 PM，也可能是团队里别的任何人。但重要的是会邀请一堆人，尤其是那些我们可能在他们地盘上做实验的其他团队的干系人——而且那不会是他们第一次知道这事。我们其实想把他们拉进来一起共同设计实验计划，好让他们完全 onboard。但绝对把他们邀请进那些实验和评审真的很关键。如果我们要在那个地盘上跑一个实验，我们需要确保实验计划里一切都是滴水不漏的，尤其是从排期角度，因为我们最不想要的就是：实验跑了一周半，那个地盘上发生了某个变化，产品团队不知道有实验在进行，直接把实验完全 invalidated 了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. And then in terms of just org wise, do you have a lieutenant that is responsible for just say the product team and then someone responsible for the growth team or the directors report up to you and you have a bunch of reports? How's that structure?
turns.zh: 酷。然后组织上，你有没有一个副手负责产品团队、再有人负责增长团队，还是总监们汇报给你、你有一堆直接下属？那结构是怎么样的？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Oh, so our CPO on the exec team [inaudible 01:12:43], he runs the entire product organization. He has four, I want to say VPs, that own different areas. So there's a couple of VPs that own different areas of the product. So first of all, our application security products. Secondly, our cloud security products. Third is platform. And fourth is what we call developer journeys, which is the area I own, which has a few groups within there, one of which being the growth group.
turns.zh: 哦，我们 exec 团队里的 CPO[听不清 01:12:43] 他管整个产品组织。他有四个，我想说是 VP，拥有不同领域。所以有几个 VP 拥有产品的不同领域。第一，我们的应用安全产品。第二，我们的云安全产品。第三是平台。第四是我们叫“开发者旅程”的，那是我拥有的领域，里面有好几个组，其中一个就是增长组。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Okay. Makes sense. Okay. There's just a couple more questions I want to ask that are very tactical specific before we get to a very exciting lightning round to close this out. One is with a freemium product, there's always this question of what to put into free and what to put into the paid plan. Is there anything you've learned about how to think about that? What should be in free and what should be behind a paywall?
turns.zh: 明白了。好。有道理。好。在进很刺激的快问快答收尾之前，还有几个非常战术、具体的问题我想问。一个是，免费增值产品总有个问题：什么放进免费、什么放进付费套餐。你有没有学到关于怎么思考这个的什么？什么该免费、什么该在付费墙后？

turns.speaker: Ben Williams
turns.en: Was it on your show with Elena that she talked about things that promote your growth model being good to land in free and things that add friction? So I really like that guidance. I'll add that for many businesses there might be some cost of service element to consider as well. Providing a feature to free users is cost prohibitive due to the volume, then that's obviously something you're going to want to reserve for paid. Ultimately, that was the whole reason cited behind Heroku, recently removing their free plain entirely. I think your plans from free to the top, they should have well defined understanding of the target customer, the use cases they should map out or you should map out the motivations for motion between each. You're really clear about what are the drivers for someone to take a step from one plan to the next. For Snyk, the real drivers to move from free to a paid plan, for example, is when you want to secure business critical code and you start having needs around governance and compliance. (01:14:39): I think the other interesting dimension is of how you approach trials. Like with most things. I think we're still figuring that out at Snyk. I don't know that there's ever a perfect answer or even a correct answer here. Certainly different from product to product. We have a self-serve trial to support time box evaluation of some of the capabilities that are reserved for our paid plans. But we're intentional in revisiting the model periodically. It's important I think to regularly challenge yourselves to ensure you don't fall into the trap of simply assuming what was best fit in the past is best fit now and in the future. What if the trial duration was limited by some dimension of usage instead of time? Or what if we didn't have a trial at all but put more into the free plan with appropriate limits? How might making those changes impact our growth model? (01:15:27): It's not always easy to answer those questions, but I think there are some ways that you could can help test there for example. You might cohort trial users and teams who have low engagement and don't convert during the trial and then when the trial ends, drop them back into a new enhanced freak plan and monitor engagement there. So there're some things you do, but I think that habit of continuously challenging yourselves and reevaluating whether the model, the specific delineations between the plans and how you support evaluation and the motion between those plans, I think it's really important to do that. And also when it comes to PLG and sales, we talked about the self-serve motion. Obviously, it's big and important for Snyk, but the sales led motion critically large as well and significantly impactful. You need to think about the plan design and those motions across both aspects of PLG and the sales led motion. When you have a strong PLG foundation that is inclusive of a product-led sales motion, you're going to be in a really powerful position from the perspective of having a significant volume of highly qualified leads that are coming from the product. We actually track a metric that we call product-driven revenue, which basically accounts for all revenue in customers where we saw meaningful value-based activity in the product before there was any sales contact. And that really tells actually a super interesting story about the PLG efficiency of your company across all revenue channels, self-serve and sales-led. And what's fascinating there is that the product-driven cohort contribute a relatively greater amount to net retention. So when you think about packaging, you know really need to think about and understand that macro level contribution of the freemium motion and know what you're trying to optimize for balancing revenue today versus potential future revenue.
turns.zh: 是不是在你和 Elena 那期，她聊了“促进你增长模型的东西适合放在免费、增加摩擦的东西……”所以我很喜欢那个指引。我补充一点：对很多企业，可能还要考虑服务成本这个维度。如果一个功能因为量大、提供给免费用户成本高到不划算，那显然是你想要留给付费的。说到底，那就是 Heroku 最近完全移除免费层背后的全部原因。我觉得你的套餐从免费到顶级，它们应该对你目标客户、用例有清晰的定义，或者你该规划出每个之间的动机。你对“一个人为什么从一层套餐走到下一层”非常清楚。对 Snyk，从免费走到付费套餐的真正驱动力，比如，是当你想保护业务关键代码、并开始有治理和合规方面的需求时。(01:14:39) 我觉得另一个有趣的维度，是你怎么 approach 试用。像大多数事一样。我觉得我们在 Snyk 还在摸索。我不知道这里有没有完美的、甚至正确的答案。肯定因产品而异。我们有一个自助试用，来支持对留给付费套餐的一些能力做限时评估。但我们刻意定期重访那个模型。我觉得定期挑战自己很重要，确保你不会掉进“想当然认为过去最 fit 的现在和未来也最 fit”的陷阱。如果试用时长不是被时间、而是被使用的某个维度限制呢？或者如果我们根本没有试用、而是把更多放进免费套餐、加上恰当的限制呢？做那些改变会怎么影响我们的增长模型？(01:15:27) 那些问题不总是好回答，但我觉得有些方式能帮你测试，比如。你可以把试用里低互动、没转化的用户和团队做成队列，等试用结束，把他们掉回一个新的增强免费套餐，并监测那里的互动。所以有你能做的事，但我认为持续挑战自己、重估那个模型、套餐之间的具体划分、以及你怎么支持评估和套餐之间的打法的习惯，真的很重要。而且在 PLG 和销售上，我们聊了自助打法。显然，它对 Snyk 又大又重要，但销售驱动的打法同样关键地大、且影响显著。你需要从 PLG 和销售驱动这两个方面去思考套餐设计和那些打法。当你有强的 PLG 基础、且包含产品驱动销售打法时，你会在“拥有大量来自产品的高度合格线索”这点上处于真正有力的位置。我们其实追踪一个叫“产品驱动收入”的指标，它基本囊括了所有这样的客户收入：在有任何销售接触之前，我们在产品里看到了有意义、基于价值的活动。而那真的讲了一个关于你公司跨所有收入渠道（自助和销售驱动）的 PLG 效率的、超级有趣的故事。那里迷人的是：产品驱动的队列对净留存贡献相对更大。所以当你想打包时，你真的需要思考并理解免费增值打法在宏观层面的贡献，并知道你在优化什么——平衡今天收入和潜在未来收入。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is that increase in net revenue retention from product-led leads mostly because they start at a cheaper price, do you think? Or is it more that they just end up being better customers?
turns.zh: 那个净收入留存的提升，主要来自产品驱动的线索起价更便宜，你觉得？还是更多因为他们最终成了更好的客户？

turns.en: No problem.

turns.en: I'm still trying to figure that out.
